titulo: Safety and efficacy of the feed additive 5-methyl-2-phenylhex-2-enal [05.099] belonging to chemical group 22 for all animal species (FEFANA asbl)
extracto: Following a request from the European Commission, EFSA was asked to deliver a scientific opinion on the safety and efficacy of 5‐methyl‐2‐phenylhex‐2‐enal [05.099] belonging to chemical group 22 (aryl‐substituted primary alcohol, aldehyde, acid, ester and acetal derivatives), when used as a sensory additive (flavouring) in feed for all animal species. The Panel on Additives and Products or Substances used in Animal Feed (FEEDAP) concludes that 5‐methyl‐2‐phenylhex‐2‐enal [05.099] is safe at the maximum proposed use level of 0.5 mg/kg complete feed for all animal species. No safety concern would arise for the consumer from the use of the additive up to the maximum proposed use level in feed. The additive should be considered as an irritant to skin and eyes and the respiratory tract, and as a dermal and respiratory sensitiser. Exposure of users by any route is considered a risk. The use of 5‐methyl‐2‐phenylhex‐2‐enal [05.099] as a flavour in animal feed was not expected to pose a risk to the environment. Since the compound under assessment is used in food as flavouring and its function in feed is essentially the same as that in food, no further demonstration of efficacy was considered necessary.

titulo: Assessment of new information on genetically modified maize MON 89034
extracto: Genetically modified (GM) maize MON 89034 expresses two insecticidal proteins, Cry1A.105 and Cry2Ab2, to confer protection against certain lepidopteran pests. This event was previously assessed by the GMO Panel as a single event and as part of multiple stacks and was found to be as safe as its conventional counterpart and the tested non‐GM reference varieties with respect to potential effects on human health, animal health and the environment. On April 2026, the European Commission requested EFSA to evaluate new N‐terminal amino acid sequence information, structural modelling and bioinformatic analysis which revealed that the Cry2Ab2 is expressed in maize MON 89034 in two variants (Cry2Ab2.820 and Cry2Ab2.820.1) differing by one N‐terminal amino acid. The sequence difference does not affect the conserved protein core, or the expected mode of action. The updated bioinformatic analyses identified no significant similarities of the newly characterised protein variant to known toxins, allergens or immunogenic gluten‐related epitopes. Thus, the EFSA GMO Panel concludes that the new information provided by the applicant on maize MON 89034 does not alter EFSA's previous conclusions. This information will be taken into account in the ongoing assessments of events containing the single maize event MON 89034.

titulo: Safety and efficacy of feed additives consisting of tinctures from Rosa canina L.: Rosehip shell tincture for horses and rosehip tincture for all animal species (FEFANA asbl)
extracto: Following a request from the European Commission, EFSA was asked to deliver a scientific opinion on the safety and efficacy of two tinctures obtained from the rosehip shells (rosehip shell tincture) or rosehip (rosehip tincture) of Rosa canina L. when used as sensory additives. The additives are water/ethanol tinctures, with a specified dry matter content of up to 11.0% (w/w) (for rosehip shell tincture) and in the range of 0.75%–1.80% (w/w) (for rosehip tincture). Rosehip shell tincture is proposed for use in feed for horses, while rosehip tincture is intended for use in feed or water for drinking for all animal species. The EFSA Panel on Additives and Products or Substances used in Animal Feed (FEEDAP) concluded that rosehip shell tincture is safe for horses at the maximum proposed use level of 2000 mg/kg complete feed. Rosehip tincture is safe for horses at the maximum proposed use level of 500 mg/kg complete feed and for all other animal species at 50 mg/kg complete feed. The FEEDAP Panel considered that the use of rosehip tincture in water for drinking alone or in combination with its use in feed is safe provided that the daily amount resulting from the exposure via feed alone at the maximum use level is not exceeded. No safety concern would arise for the consumer and the environment from the use of rosehip shell tincture or rosehip tincture in feed. The additives under assessment should be considered as irritant to skin and eyes and as dermal and respiratory sensitisers. Exposure of users by any route is considered a risk. Since rosehip preparations are recognised to flavour food and their function in feed would be essentially the same as that in food, no further demonstration of efficacy is considered necessary for rosehip shell tincture and rosehip tincture.

titulo: Wild boar-related factors relevant to African swine fever epidemiology, surveillance and control in the European Union
extracto: This report evaluates wild boar movement and behaviour, wild boar carcass search and dating, and factors associated with wild boar density and African swine fever (ASF) epidemiology. titulo: Update of the risk assessment on dioxins and dioxin-like PCBs in feed and food
extracto: The European Commission asked EFSA to update its 2018 risk assessment on polychlorinated dibenzo‐p‐dioxins and dibenzofurans (PCDD/Fs) and dioxin‐like polychlorinated biphenyls (DL‐PCBs) in feed and food, based on the 2022 WHO Toxic Equivalency Factors (WHO 2022 ‐TEFs). A decrease in sperm concentrations as a consequence of early‐life exposure was still considered the critical effect in rodents and humans. This can only be prevented by ensuring sufficiently low exposure to PCDD/Fs and DL‐PCBs of future mothers. Using the WHO 2022 ‐TEFs, the critical human study in the 2018 Opinion still showed a significant inverse association between PCDD/Fs and sperm concentration, but not when including DL‐PCBs. Therefore, this study was not used to derive a Tolerable Weekly intake (TWI). Instead, a developmental study with TCDD in rats was used to derive a TWI of 0.6 pg. WHO 2022 ‐toxic equivalents (TEQ)/kg bw per week, based on decreased sperm production. Human studies were used as supporting evidence, including an evaluation of necessary uncertainty factors. Dietary exposure assessment based on occurrence data in food from the last decade, showed that using the new TEFs resulted in 27%–35% lower total‐TEQ exposure. Mean exposure (lower to upper bound) to PCDD/Fs and DL‐PCBs for European adult populations varied between 1.87 and 6.10 pg. WHO 2022 ‐TEQ/kg bw per week, and at the P95 between 4.15 and 12.0 pg. WHO 2022 ‐TEQ/kg bw per week. The CONTAM Panel concluded that exposure for European women of childbearing age raises a health concern for their sons at the mean (80%–90% certainty) and P95 (95%–99% certainty) exposure. Including uncertainties regarding the TEFs for DL‐PCBs decreased this certainty. Human milk data confirmed the exceedance of the TWI but to a lesser extent than dietary exposure. The change in TEFs does not affect the transfer rates of individual congeners but it could impact the transfer rates when using Total‐TEQ levels.

titulo: Model development to predict environmental concentrations of chemical substances in marine sediment when the substance is applied via feed in marine aquaculture: Task 1.4. Model setup and analysis
extracto: The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) assesses the safety of fish feed additives used in aquaculture. To evaluate their potential environmental risks, it is essential to calculate the predicted environmental concentrations (PEC) and compare them to known exposure thresholds. This report outlines the setup and analysis of a model established in earlier phases of the project to get it functioning with default data and parameter sets, and to explore its sensitivity and applicability. The model is configured using environmental input data (derived from large‐scale ocean and atmosphere models across Europe) and applies standardised parameter sets representing the most common finfish aquaculture species (salmon, sea bass, and sea bream). It is implemented within a containerised system, ensuring portability and ease of deployment across computing environments. The automated modelling pipeline is broadly applicable, although performance can be challenged in areas with complex bathymetry; in these cases, targeted adjustments to default settings and workflow configurations have been explored. Model results indicate that predicted environmental concentrations (PECs) are sensitive to specific parameters, particularly those governing sediment consolidation and additive mixing depth. These parameters should therefore be prioritised in future calibration and validation efforts. The approach adopts high‐resolution, process‐based modelling across a range of representative environmental conditions to derive PEC estimates. Compared with more simplified (idealised) modelling approaches, this framework better reflects real‐world conditions, enables direct comparison with site‐specific observations, and produces outputs that are more readily interpretable for end users and decision‐makers. However, these advantages come with practical challenges, including the need to ensure robust automation across diverse environmental settings and the potential for bias in the selection of representative sites.
